procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated January 14, 1963 of the Punjab High Court in Letters Patent Appeal No. 36-D
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent challenged the order of his removal by a writ petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution. The single judge of the High Court who heard the petition opined that the General Manager was not right in holding on the material on record that the first charge is established and on the second charge he held that the General Manager's direction as per his letter of June 19, 1956 is void as being violative of Art. 19(1) of the Constitution. On appeal the appellate court upheld the conclusion of the learned single judge on the first charge but it was unable to accept his finding that the order of the General Manager of June 19, 1956 was violative of Art. 19(1) of the Constitution. All the same it affirmed the decision of the learned single judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The findings of the learned single judge as well as the judges of the appellate court were challenged before the Supreme Court by the appellant after obtaining from the High-Court a certificate under Art. 132 and 133(1)(c) of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercise of certiorari jurisdiction can interfere with finding of disciplinary authority.

facts: A railway employee was subjected to a disciplinary inquiry on two charges.
An enquiry committee concluded that the first charge was not proved, but the second was.

The disciplinary authority (the General Manager) disagreed with the committee on the first charge. He accepted the evidence of two witnesses, which the committee had rejected, and found the employee guilty of the first charge as well.
The High Court, exercising its writ jurisdiction, interfered with and set aside the General Manager's finding on the first charge.
law: The Supreme Court established that a disciplinary authority is not bound by the conclusions reached by an enquiry committee and is free to reach its own findings based on the evidence on record.

A High Court, in its certiorari jurisdiction, can only interfere with the finding of a disciplinary authority if the finding is not supported by any evidence or if it is a finding that no reasonable person could have reached (i.e., it is perverse).
application: The Supreme Court noted that the General Manager's finding on the first charge was based on the evidence of two witnesses who stated that the employee had compelled them to shut down a compressor.
The Court found that this constituted evidence in support of the disciplinary authority's conclusion.
It further determined that the conclusion reached by the General Manager was not one that no reasonable person could have arrived at.
Since the finding was supported by evidence and was not perverse, the necessary conditions for the High Court to interfere were not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had exceeded its powers under its certiorari jurisdiction by interfering with the disciplinary authority's conclusion. The Court held that as long as the authority's finding was supported by some evidence and was not unreasonable, it must prevail and could not be interfered with by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order of removal based on a number of grounds, of which one is not sustainable, is liable to be struck down.

facts: A railway employee was removed from service based on two charges.
The High Court's appellate division held that if an order of removal is based on multiple grounds and one of them is found to be unsustainable, the entire order is liable to be struck down.
The reasoning was that it is difficult to know to what extent the authority's decision was based on the invalid ground.
law: The Supreme Court relied on its previous decision in *State of Orissa v. Bidyabhan Mohapatra*.

The legal principle established is that if an order in a disciplinary enquiry (under Art. 311) can be supported by any single finding of a "substantial misdemeanour" for which the punishment can be lawfully imposed, the order is valid.
application: The Court rejected the High Court's reasoning.
It held that it is not the Court's role to consider whether the disciplinary authority would have imposed the same punishment based on the remaining valid ground alone.
As long as the punishment can be legally justified by at least one of the proven charges, the order should be upheld.
In this case, it was not disputed that the first charge was serious enough on its own to warrant the punishment of removal from service.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the view that a removal order based on multiple grounds must be struck down if one ground is unsustainable. The Court held that the order can be upheld if it can be supported by any single, proven charge that constitutes a substantial misdemeanour for which the imposed punishment is lawful.

issue.issue_text: Whether the direction by the General Manager of the Railway prohibiting meetings within railway premises was violative of Art. 19(1)(a), (b), and (c) of the Constitution.

facts: The General Manager of the Northern Railway issued a direction prohibiting employees from holding meetings within railway premises, including workshops, depots, and open grounds.
An employee, who was also a trade union worker, was charged and removed from service for violating this direction by addressing several meetings within the railway premises.

The employee challenged this direction, arguing it violated his fundamental rights to freedom of speech, peaceful assembly, and to form associations under Article 19(1)(a), (b), and (c) of the Constitution.
law: The fundamental rights to freedom of speech, peaceful assembly, and to form associations or unions under Article 19(1) are not absolute.

A property owner, including a State Undertaking like the Indian Railways, has the right to enjoy and control its property in the same manner as a private individual, subject only to restrictions imposed by law or usage.
There is no fundamental right for any citizen to hold meetings or exercise their freedom of speech on property belonging to someone else.
application: The Court established that the Northern Railway was the owner of the premises in question.
It reasoned that the General Manager's direction did not take away the workers' fundamental freedoms but merely prohibited the exercise of those freedoms *within* the railway's property.

The Court held that the freedoms guaranteed under Article 19(1) do not grant citizens the right to exercise them in any place they choose. The exercise of these rights ends where the property rights of another person begin.

This limitation, based on property rights, is considered inherent in the fundamental rights themselves. Therefore, the validity of the direction did not need to be judged by the tests of 'reasonable restrictions' found in sub-articles (2), (3), and (4) of Article 19.
The Court found no law or established usage that gave railway employees a right to hold meetings on railway premises. It noted that allowing such a right could lead to chaos in offices.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the General Manager's direction was not violative of Article 19(1)(a), (b), or (c). The prohibition was a valid exercise of the Railway's right as a property owner to control the use of its premises, and it did not infringe upon the employees' fundamental rights, which could be exercised elsewhere.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercise of certiorari jurisdiction can interfere with finding of disciplinary authority.
appellant_arguments: The High Court exceeded its powers by interfering with the findings of the disciplinary authority (the General Manager).

The disciplinary authority was not bound by the conclusions of the Enquiry Committee and was entitled to reach its own finding, as long as it was supported by some evidence and was a conclusion a reasonable person could reach.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's interference was justified because the disciplinary authority's finding, which overturned the enquiry committee's conclusion, was not sustainable. (Inferred from the High Court's initial ruling in the respondent's favor).

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order of removal based on a number of grounds, of which one is not sustainable, is liable to be struck down.
appellant_arguments: The punishment order can be sustained even if one of the two charges is found to be unsustainable.
If the order can be supported by a finding of a substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can be lawfully imposed, the court should not interfere.
respondent_arguments: The punishment order cannot be sustained and must be struck down if one of the charges on which it is based is found to be unsustainable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the direction by the General Manager of the Railway prohibiting meetings within railway premises was violative of Art. 19(1)(a), (b), and (c) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The direction prohibiting meetings within railway premises was a valid restriction and not a violation of Article 19. (Inferred from the General Manager's action and the court's final decision).
respondent_arguments: The rights to freedom of speech, peaceful assembly, and to form associations under Art. 19(1)(a), (b), and (c) are inviolable.
The General Manager's direction interfered with these rights.
Railway workers have a right to assemble in any place they choose.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: There is no fundamental right to hold meetings on government property, as the exercise of freedoms like speech and assembly is inherently limited by the property rights of others. If a disciplinary order imposing punishment is based on multiple charges, it will be upheld if it can be supported by a finding of a substantial misdemeanour on any single charge for which the imposed punishment is lawful. A court cannot interfere with the findings of a disciplinary authority unless the finding is not supported by any evidence or is one that no reasonable person could have reached.
obiter: The more an owner, for his advantage, opens up his property for use by the public in general, the more do his rights become circumscribed by the statutory and constitutional rights of those who use it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that fundamental rights under Article 19 are not absolute and do not grant citizens the right to hold meetings on any property they choose, as these rights are circumscribed by the property rights of others, including the government. Consequently, the General Manager's direction prohibiting meetings on railway premises was valid. The court also established that a disciplinary order based on multiple charges can be sustained even if one charge fails, provided it is supported by a finding on a substantial misdemeanour, and that the High Court, in its certiorari jurisdiction, cannot interfere with the disciplinary authority's findings of fact if they are supported by some evidence.
legal_tests_applied: Freedom of speech, freedom to assemble peac&-fully and the freedom to form Associations or Unions does not mean that these rights can be exercised by the citizen• in whatever place they please. The exercise of those freedoms will come to an end as soon as the right of some one else to hold rus prop<;rty intervenes. Such a limitation is inherent in the exercise of those nghts.

It was open to the General Manager to accept the evidence which the Enquiry Committee had rejected on the first charge and he was not bound by the conclusions reached by the com[mittee].
